wells.key_finding: Well BO014 (BNKO00014 / O-W1-44) is an idle ESP-equipped producer in the Bangko Field that has been shut in since September 2005 due to high water cut and pump failure, with the last well test recording 98% WC on all open completions — a confirmed knockout condition under the screening criteria. The primary producing interval (1600 SD) is likely depleted based on offset well BO233 results, and the 1740 SD tested dry across multiple attempts, leaving the 1710 SD sand (1,725–1,760 ft) as the only viable reactivation target, supported by a November 2000 swab test that showed oil flow at 86% WC with a FAP estimate of 100–150 BOPD on file. The overall screening score of 29/60 (average 2.42) places this well at LOW priority with a knockout risk, and the realistic post-workover oil rate from the 1710 SD is estimated at only 10–30 BOPD — a marginal economic case that does not justify a workover commitment unless an RST/PNL confirms residual oil saturation in the 1710 SD, a current integrity survey clears the wellbore and ESP hardware after 20+ years idle, and a formal nodal analysis confirms the rate clears the economic threshold

wells.key_finding: BO149 is a long-life Bangko Field producer with a production history spanning from at least late 1997 through March 2013, with a peak monthly oil allocation of approximately 4,741 Bbls in October 2006, but by the time it was shut in, the well had declined to just 4.6 BOPD at a calculated water cut of 99.8%, producing 2,229 BFPD total fluid of which only 68 Bbls of oil was recovered over 15 active days in its final producing month. The well has been idle since April 2013, now over 13 years, and the production data alone suggests the shutdown was driven by uneconomic oil rate at extreme water cut rather than a mechanical failure, though this cannot be confirmed because no well file, completion record, workover history, perforation data, integrity log, or well test data was provided in this dataset. This data absence is the single most critical problem: without knowing the reservoir zone, completion type, artificial lift condition, and wellbore integrity status, it is impossible to reliably assess whether BO149 has any reactivation potential, whether a behind-pipe or by-passed zone exists, or what intervention scope would be required, and the entire well file must be retrieved from the CPI operator data room before this well can advance beyond a preliminary idle well flag.

wells.key_finding:
BM020 is not a straightforward reactivation candidate. The well has a clear and executable workover proposal from PE (WSO04), a known target (upper MN3160 sand), and the intervention cause (water coning) is understood.[1]
However, three critical data items must be resolved before the well can be moved to Priority 1:
•	A PNL/RST saturation log must confirm remaining oil saturation above the water cone. Without this, there is no direct evidence that the 5 ft re-perforation target at 3280–3285 ft contains producible oil.
•	A current reservoir pressure survey is needed to validate whether the formation can deliver economically at 30 BOPD.
•	A surface inspection must confirm the wellhead and flow line are in acceptable condition.
If the PNL/RST confirms residual oil and reservoir pressure supports at least 20–30 BOPD deliverability, the well should be promoted to Priority 1. The workover scope is defined, the field infrastructure is established, and the intervention cost is within a reasonable range for a 30 BOPD oil gain target. The investment decision depends on oil price assumptions and the cost-to-gain ratio, which should be evaluated with a full economic model after the validation data is collected.

wells.key_finding: CA006 is a viable but conditional reactivation candidate. The well produced consistently at 40–75 BOPD for roughly eight years after a 2007 workover, confirming the Menggala SD reservoir can sustain commercial rates under ESP lift. The current idle status is driven entirely by water flooding of the existing perforations, not by structural depletion or mechanical failure, and the 2014 re-perforation event proved that unswept oil existed in adjacent intervals as recently as 11 years ago. A 90 ft gross Menggala SD interval at 2770–2860 ft was explicitly identified in the 2003 completion recommendation as unproduced and never perforated, making it the primary behind-pipe target. The well carries the highest data completeness score of all wells assessed in this screening program, supported by a 2003 CHFR cased-hole resistivity log, a confirmed cement bond, 12 years of production history, and a 2022 seven-formation structure map set. The single action that resolves the key uncertainty is a PNL run through the existing completion to confirm current oil saturation in that unperforated interval. If movable oil is confirmed, the technical case for a full workover reactivation is sound.

wells.key_finding: Well FAJAR-0002D1 (FJ002, O-O-44A/B-02) is a directional oil producer in the Pematang Formation (URB sub-zone), Fajar Field, Bekasap SBU, Riau, Sumatra, operated by PT Chevron Pacific Indonesia. The well has been idle since September 2008, approximately 17 years, with the immediate shutdown reason being pump failure and the root cause being a critically low PI of 0.3 BFPDpsi confirmed in April 2007. Despite this, the last recorded well test in September 2008, after a multi-zone reperforation campaign across seven Pematang URB intervals between 7,068 and 7,574 ft MD, showed an encouraging post-reperforation rate of approximately 502 BOPD at only 4% water cut, suggesting residual reservoir deliverability exists if the PI issue can be addressed. A January 2012 well service program proposed a low-cost swab and rod pump installation (D475N at 7,390 ft) with an estimated cost of only USD 40,000 and an expected oil gain of 30 BOPD, but no evidence of execution exists in the file set. Well integrity appears moderate with no confirmed casing or tubing leak on record, PBTD at 7,668 ft was accessible in 2008, and CBL from the 2001 completion indicates acceptable cement quality, though no post-2012 integrity verification has been performed. Location access is good with established Fajar Field infrastructure, and the Bekasap SBU gathering system is confirmed active, but current reservoir pressure, an updated PI measurement, a current integrity survey, and facility capacity data are all missing, making this well a Medium Priority candidate that requires low-cost diagnostic work before any intervention commitment

wells.key_finding: Gulamo-001 (O-O-44) is a mature Pematang formation ESP producer in the Gulamo Field, Balam Asset, onshore Riau Sumatra, drilled in 1988 and completed in 1996 as the field discovery well, with cumulative production of 140,454 BO by November 2015 when it was placed on preventive maintenance shutdown. The well has been producing at greater than 97% water cut since 2006 and reached 99.9% WC on its last recorded test in October 2015, which is a knockout condition under the screening framework. Despite having multiple Pematang sand intervals between 4930 sd and 6440 sd, virtually all perforated zones are confirmed wet, with most previously squeezed off using cement or isolated with lockset packers. The only credible remaining opportunity is the unperforated PM 4980 sd interval, which shows 40 ohm-m resistivity on the marked log and has never been individually tested, plus potential bypass oil in shallower sands identified near the offset Ganda-01 location. Historical workover costs have been low, consistently below USD 200,000 per program using a hoist and wireline unit, and the wellbore is confirmed accessible to near-PBTD at 6494 ft based on 2014 data. However, no current BHP measurement, CBL/VDL, RST or PNL saturation log, or post-2015 site inspection exists in the available file set, leaving the reservoir pressure, cement integrity, remaining saturation, and surface facility condition all unverified. This well is currently classified as Tier 3 / Low Priority with a Knockout Risk flag on water cut, and reactivation should not be sanctioned until individual zone swab testing of PM 4980 sd and a current integrity and saturation survey confirm measurable oil potential above the economic threshold.

wells.key_finding: INTA00004 (S1-O-26) holds a viable reactivation pathway with well-defined workover scope, established facility connectivity, and an estimated cost well under USD 150,000, which makes it a low-cost candidate relative to most idle well interventions. However, the current screening places it at Priority 2 because three data gaps carry enough technical risk to defer commitment: the BK 2900 sd and BK 3050 sd swab rates date back to 1999 and have never been re-confirmed, no SBHP or pressure survey exists post-2010 to validate reservoir energy for a new ESP design, and no reserve estimate or CO log saturation interpretation is available to confirm the remaining oil volume justifies the spend. The priority outcome is directly tied to the swab test result on the two candidate zones — if either zone delivers above 30 BOPD at manageable water cut, the well upgrades to Priority 1 with a clear and low-cost execution path; if both zones return high water cut, the economic case collapses and the well drops to Priority 3.

wells.key_finding: JORA00019 is a Priority 2 candidate with real reactivation potential, supported by significant historical production, an underdepleted Menggala lower zone, good surface infrastructure, and an established ESP lift system. The well cannot advance to Priority 1 until five critical data items are confirmed: a wellhead physical inspection, a static pressure gradient run, RST or PNL on the Menggala 5100 SD and 5160 SD intervals, a CBL check across the previously squeezed Bekasap and Bangko intervals, and a current cost estimate from a qualified workover contractor. The water cut knockout (Score 1) driven by 94–99% WC from the active Bekasap perforations is the single blocking factor, and it can only be resolved by confirming residual oil saturation in the Menggala lower lobes and verifying cement isolation integrity before any workover commitment is made. Once this data package is in hand, a definitive reclassification to Priority 1 or Priority 3 can be made with full technical confidence.

Technically, the causes are a combination of:  
1. Low fluid rate, although the water cut is around 90%. In records, a 90% water cut is still referred to as “still good around 90% WC”, but the total fluid rate is already low.

5. The structure position of Kerang 02 is said to be on the flank and almost 100 ft lower than Kerang #01, so the remaining oil potential is considered uncertain. The well shut in due to economics, not mechanical failure, which is a positive starting point. However, three critical unknowns block any commitment: current reservoir pressure is unmeasured since 2003, no saturation log exists to confirm moveable oil in the lower Bangko and Menggala sands, and the wellbore has had no entry since the 1997 CBL run. Before spending any workover budget, run a pulsed neutron log (RST or C/O) to confirm residual oil saturation, conduct a static BHP survey on the next wellbore entry, and perform a wellhead integrity check. If those three data points confirm oil saturation above 40% in at least one zone and reservoir pressure above 40% of original, the well moves to Priority 1 with a hoist-class workover scope estimated under USD 1 million at current cost levels. The path forward requires a current wellhead inspection and pressure test, a slickline drift run to confirm PBTD access and quantify sand fill, a static pressure gradient survey to establish reservoir energy, and an RST or PNL saturation check to identify whether any bypassed oil or behind-pipe zone remains in the Petani AMT or Menggala stack, and only if those steps return positive results should a revised workover concept and AFE be prepared.

The 2013 reactivation campaign (PMP16) attempted to manage coning by down-sizing the ESP and reducing drawdown, but the well returned zero oil and was shut in again by late 2014. The screening matrix scores the well at 29 out of 55 scored points, placing it in LOW priority with a Knockout Risk flag driven by the complete absence of any saturation log (RST or PNL) to confirm whether residual oil still exists in the horizontal section. The single most important technical question before any further investment is whether the horizontal wellbore still holds recoverable oil, because without that confirmation, every other parameter, cost, lift design, and workover scope, is academic. The well has been idle for approximately 12 years, which is long enough for the water cone to have partially receded, so it warrants a low-cost saturation log run before being written off entirely.

wells.key_finding: MINA01903 (3B-52) is a directional oil producer in the Minas Field, Riau, that was drilled and completed in early 2013 but never achieved commercial production. The well perforated A1 and A2 sands, yet water cut was already at 98.4% in its very first producing month and climbed to 99.92% by the time it was shut in after January 2021. Peak oil rate across its entire producing life was only 30.3 BOPD in April 2013, and by last production it had collapsed to 2.0 BOPD, indicating the oil productivity index had declined to less than 10% of its original value. Three interventions between 2013 and 2018 confirmed the wellbore is mechanically sound with no casing damage, no fish, and full access to 2762 ft, and the intervention cost would be well below USD 0.50M, so the well is not a mechanical problem. The core issue is reservoir-side: the A1 and A2 sands are aquifer-dominated and essentially spent for current perforations. The only remaining technical upside is the unperforated B1 and B2 sands at 2686 ft and 2738 ft, which were logged and identified at completion but never tested. Before any abandonment decision is made, a wireline RST or PNL run to evaluate residual oil saturation in B1 and B2 is the single most valuable next action. If those zones confirm bypassed oil, the well has a re-perforation case. If not, it should move directly to abandonment screening

wells.key_finding: Pematang Bow #3 is a vertical oil producer in the Lower Sihapas Formation, Duri District, Riau, that has been idle for approximately 53 years following a confirmed primary cement failure and behind-casing water crossflow from the Upper Sihapas sands. The well produced briefly from June 1972 to April 1973, reaching a peak of around 2,500 BOPD field allocation before declining rapidly to 31 BOPD at 88% water cut within seven months, then collapsing to 98-100% water cut after a routine pump change in February 1973 triggered uncontrolled water entry from an unperforated zone. The root cause is poor primary cement, confirmed by CBL showing bonding in only two short intervals (4,312-4,380 ft and 4,450-4,456 ft) out of a 5,185 ft production string, leaving the productive R/S and M/N sands in an uncemented section throughout the well's entire producing life. All lifting equipment, tubing, and rods were removed in July 1973, no current pressure, integrity, or reserve data exists, and the well sits 37 ft structurally below the up-dip producer PB#1 in a water-invaded field. With two active Knockout flags on Integrity Risk and Artificial Lift, a total screening score of 19 out of 60, and no subsurface data to support a current oil gain forecast, this well is not a reactivation candidate in its present state and should be evaluated for P&A before any capital is committed.

wells.key_finding: PUNC00032D1 (Puncak 32, O-O-65) is a directional ESP producer that has never delivered commercial oil. The Menggala primary zone was watered out from first perforation in April 2008, producing 100% WC from day one, which immediately triggered a supplement program to perforate Bangko and Bekasap. Despite three completions over nine years across four intervals, the well never exceeded 14.3 BOPD annual average and produced a cumulative total of only 12,769 barrels (12.8 Mbbl) against an original target of 200-400 BOPD. Water cut was above 97% in every single production year, and the well shut down naturally in January 2018 at 0.80 BOPD and 99.89% WC. The current PBTD is confirmed at only 1,543.5 ft versus the original 2,240 ft, meaning the Bangko zone at 2,056-2,064 ft and the Menggala zone at 2,142-2,175 ft are both buried behind sand fill and completely inaccessible without a full CTU cleanout workover. No CBL has been run since 2008, no current pressure survey exists, and no dual barrier has been verified, leaving the integrity status of the production casing unknown after 17 years of high-salinity water production. The only accessible perforation is the upper Bekasap at 1,282-1,292 ft added in April 2017, but this zone showed no meaningful oil response and produced at the same near-100% WC as all other intervals. There is currently no confirmed productive zone, no current well test data, and no reserve estimate in any file in the folder. The well is Priority 3, Low, and should not receive capital until a CTU cleanout restores lower wellbore access, individual zone tests confirm WC below 95% in at least one interval, and a current pressure survey establishes whether any reservoir energy remains.

The well was drilled in 2009 as a development well targeting the Menggala sand in Puncak Field, but it failed to deliver economic oil production from day one because all four perforated intervals — Duri B, BKO 1970, BKO 2020, and Menggala — were aquifer-dominated from initial completion, with only BKO 1970 showing a brief oil response at 60% WC on first swab before deteriorating to 97.4% WC by May 2013 and 100% WC by August 2014. The well scores 27 out of 60 in the 12-parameter screening matrix, carries a Knockout flag on Workover Complexity because a full rig is required as the minimum re-entry scope, and is classified as Priority 3 — meaning no workover capital should be allocated until three low-cost data-acquisition steps are completed: a carbon-oxygen log or RST survey on BKO 1970 to confirm whether any movable oil remains, a shut-in pressure measurement to establish current reservoir energy, and an individual zone swab test on BKO 1970 isolated from the two confirmed water-only zones below it.

wells.key_finding: Singa 1 (SING00001) was drilled in 1976 to test a Duri L-Sand structural closure, but the well encountered a fundamental reservoir problem from the start. The only productive oil sand was 6 ft thick, sitting directly on the oil-water contact at 2188-2193 ft, and water broke through within two months of production onset, climbing from 7% water cut in February 1977 to over 96% by December 1976 and reaching 98-99% for the remainder of its producing life. Despite multiple shut-in and test cycles conducted by the district engineer in mid-1978, including one-week, two-week, and three-week shut-in periods, water cut showed no improvement, and the well produced only 91 barrels of oil over six producing days during those tests, confirming the oil column was effectively swept. Cumulative oil production at the time of shut-in was only 9,533 BO against original field reserves of 3.2 MMBO, and the district engineer formally concluded in July 1978 that no viable oil recompletion existed in this wellbore, with the only secondary target (Petani Gas Sand at 1120-1140 ft) blocked by the absence of cement behind casing confirmed on CBL. A cement squeeze was performed on the Petani interval in February 1986 (Dowell Schlumberger job), but no subsequent production test or evaluation of the gas zone was documented, and the well has remained idle with no pump in hole and no current integrity data for the 40 years since that last workover. In short, Singa 1 is a reservoir problem, not a workover opportunity. The well was drilled on a structurally marginal position with an oil column too thin to survive water influx, and reactivation as an oil producer carries no subsurface justification from the available data.

wells.key_finding: Duri 4R-65B #5219 is a slim-hole steam injector in Duri Steamflood Area 3, Riau, Indonesia, completed in 3.5-inch casing to 850 ft TD with four BJD sand perforation intervals between 674 and 782 ft. The well has a documented history of recurring sand fill above perforations, with the top of sand consistently found at 698-701 ft on every slickline and CTU job from 2006 through 2013, and a persistent mechanical restriction at approximately 710 ft that prevented the 3.5-inch casing scrapper from passing in every CTU job on record. Cement integrity was confirmed by CBL at completion in May 2000, and no tubing or casing leak has been reported in any intervention record. The last recorded operational data is from October 2013, when a spinner survey tagged at 699 ft with WHP at 138 PSI and BHT at 295 degF, and no current post-2013 status, oil production data, reservoir pressure, or reserve information exists in the provided dataset. The well scores favorably on intervention cost, accessibility, and facility readiness given Duri's mature infrastructure, but the overall assessment is limited to Medium priority because the fundamental question of whether this well contributes to oil gain, and what the remaining reserves look like in its drainage area, cannot be answered without a saturation log, reservoir pressure survey, and confirmation of the current idle status and the reason the well was shut in.

wells.key_finding: 4R-68B (#5227), Duri Field Area 3, this well is a shallow Baji sand producer with a perforation interval at 700 to 708 ft and a confirmed PBTD at 819 ft, located in an active Duri Steam Flood (DSF) pattern. The last three slickline interventions (2007, 2008, 2009) consistently confirmed wellbore accessibility down to 803 to 807 ft with only minor sand fill above PBTD, and the CBL run at initial completion in May 2000 showed good cement bonding throughout the 3.5" production casing. The most significant integrity concern is a corrosive 1" round hole found on the 3.5" casing at surface level during a 2004 wellhead changeout, which was remediated at the time, but no post-repair casing inspection has been documented since. The well scores well on intervention cost (estimated below $0.5M for slickline or CTU cleanout), site accessibility (full Duri infrastructure in place), and workover complexity (likely slickline or CTU only), but it scores poorly on data completeness because no production rate, water cut, reservoir pressure, PI, or reserve data exists in the current file set, making 11 of the 15 screening parameters low-confidence provisional scores. The overall verdict is Medium Priority (Priority 2): the mechanical and logistical conditions are favorable for a low-cost reactivation attempt, but a firm go-ahead decision requires a fresh slickline run to confirm current sand fill, a tubing integrity pressure test, retrieval of production allocation and well test history from the company database, a reservoir pressure survey, and an RST or PNL to confirm remaining oil saturation in the Baji interval before any intervention commitment is made.

wells.key_finding: the well is a shallow steam injector drilled in May 2000 to 850 ft TD in the Duri Field Area 3, targeting Jaga, Dalam, and Manggis sands in an SOR pattern, and has been shut-in since December 2007 with zero production target. The primary technical issue driving its idle status is a recurring sand fill at 646-653 ft that repeatedly returned after CTU clean-out operations in 2006 and 2007, combined with a casing scraper that could not pass 652 ft, indicating a persistent mechanical restriction at the top of the Jaga perforation interval. A 2008 recommendation proposed isolating the mature Jaga sand using a CTU-deployed tubing patch and redirecting steam to the Dalam interval, which was described as still cold and therefore potentially holding unswept oil, but there is no confirmation in the provided files that this job was ever executed. The well carries a moderate reactivation score of 45 out of 75, with the strongest upside being a relatively low estimated intervention cost below $500K USD, established Duri field surface infrastructure, and the cold Dalam and Manggis sands as a plausible production target, but a final commitment cannot be made without obtaining production history, running an RST or PNL for current saturation confirmation, and verifying current wellhead and casing integrity after more than 18 years of shut-in.
